planting.note: Plant divisions in humus-rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring, setting the crown just at soil level; keep evenly moist while new fronds establish.

directions: Japanese chain fern forms handsome clumps of glossy, leathery, once-pinnate fronds on a short, slowly creeping rhizome, making it far less aggressive in the garden than its native American cousins Virginia and netted chain fern. Plant divisions in humus-rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, where it associates well with hostas, hellebores, and other woodland perennials. It tolerates brief dry spells better than most chain ferns but colors and fronds best with steady moisture and protection from hot afternoon sun. Established clumps are evergreen to semi-evergreen in milder parts of its range and benefit from a spring cleanup of tattered winter foliage.

planting.note: Plant divisions or basal offsets in constantly moist to boggy, humus-rich soil in deep shade in spring, and keep newly set plants shaded and damp until roots establish.

directions: Fishbone water fern takes its name from the finely divided, herringbone-like arrangement of pinnae along each arching frond, and in age it slowly builds a short trunk like a miniature tree fern. Native to cool, wet forests and streambanks of southeastern Australia and New Zealand, it demands constantly moist to boggy, humus-rich soil and deep shade with high humidity, making it a natural choice for shaded bog gardens, pond margins, or fern gullies. It resents drying out even briefly and performs poorly in hot, dry climates, so site it where a cool root zone and reliable moisture can be maintained. Divide congested crowns or detach basal offsets in spring, keeping new divisions shaded and constantly damp until re-established.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade in spring, spacing to allow for its gradual spread; water in well and keep consistently moist until established.

directions: Gristle fern is a robust Australian understory species named for the unusually tough, cartilage-like texture of its frond stalks and midribs, which let it stand up to foot traffic and dry spells better than many shade ferns. New fronds emerge flushed with pink to coppery bronze before maturing to deep glossy green, adding seasonal color to shaded plantings. It spreads gradually by rhizome to form broad colonies in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil under full to partial shade, and tolerates brief dry periods once established better than most Blechnum species. Grow it as a woodland groundcover or understory drift in frost-free to lightly frosted gardens, dividing rhizome sections in spring to propagate or control its spread.

planting.note: Plant divisions in constantly wet to consistently moist, humus-rich soil in deep shade in spring, siting near a stream, pond edge, or shaded bog where moisture stays reliable.

directions: Ray water fern, known in New Zealand as kiwikiwi, produces a flattened, radiating rosette of sterile fronds pressed close to the ground with separate, more upright fertile fronds rising from the center, giving established plants a distinctive two-tiered look. It grows naturally along cool forest streambanks and demands constantly wet to consistently moist, humus-rich soil in deep shade with high humidity, thriving best where summers stay mild. Use it at pond edges, stream banks, or in shaded bog gardens rather than average border conditions, since heat and drying wind quickly scorch the delicate fronds. Divide crowded rosettes in spring, keeping divisions shaded and constantly damp until roots re-establish.

planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted plantlets in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil or potting mix in bright to deep shade with high humidity in spring; hanging baskets let the trailing fronds display naturally.

directions: Trailing maidenhair produces narrow, once-pinnate fronds that lengthen and arch downward as they mature, rooting new plantlets wherever the drooping frond tips touch moist soil, a habit that gives rise to its walking-fern nickname and makes it an easy fern to propagate and share. Grow it in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in bright to deep shade with high humidity, where its trailing habit suits hanging baskets, raised planters, and terrarium edges. It is frost-tender and reliably hardy outdoors only in humid, frost-free zone 10-11 climates; in cooler gardens grow it as a container or houseplant fern and bring it under cover before frost. Remove rooted plantlets to start new pots, and mist regularly since low humidity browns the fine foliage quickly.

planting.note: Plant divisions in humus-rich, constantly moist, well-drained soil or potting mix in bright to deep shade with high humidity in spring, protecting new divisions from direct sun and drafts while they root.

directions: Peruvian maidenhair is prized for pinnae much larger and more rounded than typical maidenhairs, unfurling with a metallic silvery-pink sheen before maturing to broad, glossy dark green leaflets on wiry black stems. Native to humid Andean cloud forests, it needs constantly moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in bright to deep shade with consistently high humidity, and it will not tolerate direct sun, dry air, or drying out between waterings. It is hardy outdoors only in frost-free zone 10-11 climates; elsewhere it makes a dramatic conservatory, terrarium, or shaded patio container specimen. Divide congested crowns in spring, keeping new divisions warm, shaded, and constantly damp until re-established.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant divisions in consistently moist to wet, calcareous or humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring, siting near a seep, spring, or shaded rain garden where moisture stays constant.

directions: Ovate maiden fern grows naturally along limestone seeps and spring-fed creek banks on the Texas Edwards Plateau and into northern Mexico, forming neat clumps of broadly ovate-lanceolate, pale yellow-green fronds that are shorter and less aggressively spreading than the related southern shield fern. Plant it in consistently moist to wet, calcareous or humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, where it tolerates the periodic flooding and constant seepage moisture of its native limestone habitat. It suits shaded rain gardens, spring-fed borders, and native plant collections in the Gulf Coast and Texas Hill Country, and is more clump-forming and better behaved in small spaces than many of its running relatives. Divide crowded clumps in spring, keeping divisions consistently moist until new fronds emerge.
sources: Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center Native Plant Database
